lessons.title: AI Office, AI Board, and Germany's authority structure
lessons.subtitle: Who actually supervises a mid-sized company: the EU level, the Federal Network Agency, and sectoral authorities

sections.title: EU level: AI Office and European AI Board
sections.content:
Six units, more than 125 staff, including Regulation and Compliance and AI Safety, housed in the European Commission's Directorate-General CNECT (Communications Networks, Content and Technology). That is the **AI Office** (European Artificial Intelligence Office).

Its remit is narrow. Over **general-purpose AI (GPAI) models** such as GPT-4, Claude, and Gemini, Article 88 gives the AI Office **exclusive supervisory powers**. It coordinates the codes of practice, runs the secretariat of the European AI Board, and has operated the public Service Desk since 8 October 2025.

The **European AI Board** sits in Article 65. One representative per Member State. It coordinates the national authorities and advises the Commission.

What follows for a company that deploys AI and places no general-purpose AI model on the market? Neither the AI Office nor the Board is normally its supervisory contact. Its contacts sit in Germany.
sections.keyTakeaway: The AI Office supervises GPAI models at EU level. The European AI Board coordinates the Member States under Article 65. For a managing director who only deploys AI, neither is the direct supervisory contact.

sections.title: Germany: the Federal Network Agency as the default authority
sections.content:
Article 70(2) requires every Member State to name a **single point of contact**. Germany has one. The German AI Market Implementation Act (KI-MIG) names the **Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur, BNetzA)**. The Bundestag adopted the Act on **11 June 2026**; on **10 July 2026** it passed the Bundesrat without referral to the Mediation Committee; it **entered into force on 29 July 2026**. The EU Regulation itself applies directly, its individual provisions on the staged schedule.

Since then the BNetzA has been the market-surveillance authority for every area without assigned sectoral supervision, and the single point of contact and complaints body. The Act provides for a **Coordination and Competence Centre (KoKIVO)** inside the agency and an independent market-surveillance chamber for specified areas.

The right reporting channel in an individual case still follows the sector and its own law. For a real case what counts is the enacted legislation, the applicable sectoral law, and current information from the authority. Not this lesson.
sections.keyTakeaway: The KI-MIG has been in force since 29 July 2026. It makes the BNetzA the single point of contact and complaints body where no sectoral authority has jurisdiction. The specific reporting route still follows the sector and its law.

sections.title: Sectoral supervision: which other authorities retain jurisdiction
sections.content:
The BNetzA is the fallback authority, not the only one. Article 74 assigns market surveillance in several areas to existing sectoral authorities. Data-protection law and other sector-specific law keep their own allocations of responsibility.

- **Financial institutions:** Article 74(6) generally refers to the authorities responsible under financial-services law.
- **Products covered by Annex I:** Market surveillance generally follows the relevant product-safety law (Article 74(3)).
- **Bodies referred to in Article 74(8):** The data-protection or other authorities named there supervise the Annex III systems specified in that paragraph.
- **Other areas in Germany:** The KI-MIG, in force since 29 July 2026, gives the BNetzA the fallback role. Check the jurisdictional provision before you rely on it.

**Implementation practice:** For every system, record purpose, role, sector, and the authorities that may have jurisdiction. Until the authorities consolidate their guidance, that mapping stays a legal question that needs confirmation.
sections.keyTakeaway: Sectoral supervision and sector-specific law stay in play. The BNetzA's fallback role follows from the KI-MIG, in force since 29 July 2026.

quiz.questionText: Which authority does the KI-MIG, in force since 29 July 2026, designate as the single point of contact under Article 70(2)?

answerOptions.text: The Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI)
The Federal Network Agency (BNetzA)
The Federal Office for Information Security (BSI)
The Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action (BMWK)

quiz.explanation: The KI-MIG has been in force since 29 July 2026 and names the Federal Network Agency as the single point of contact. Which authority is competent in an individual case still follows the sector and its law.

quiz.questionText: A bank uses an AI system for credit scoring. Which German authority is the market-surveillance authority under Article 74(6)?

answerOptions.text: BNetzA
BaFin
BfDI
DAkkS

quiz.explanation: Article 74(6) of the AI Act puts market surveillance for AI systems at financial institutions in the hands of the competent financial supervisor. In Germany that is BaFin. The same model in the HR department of the same bank falls to the BNetzA.

quiz.questionText: What is the AI Office's primary function?

answerOptions.text: Direct supervision of every AI application used by an SME
The authority responsible for fines under Article 99
Exclusive supervision of GPAI models and coordination at EU level (Article 88)
Certification of AI regulatory sandboxes in the Member States

quiz.explanation: The AI Office sits in the European Commission (DG CNECT). Article 88 gives it exclusive powers over GPAI models such as GPT-4, Claude, and Gemini. Ordinary AI use in a mid-sized company belongs to the national authorities under Article 70, in Germany mainly the BNetzA.

lessons.title: Fines of up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent
lessons.subtitle: The three penalty tiers under Article 99, and what they really mean for a company with EUR 20 million in turnover

sections.title: The three penalty tiers under Article 99
sections.content:
EUR 35 million is the number in every headline. For a small or medium-sized company it is not the ceiling. Article 99 of the AI Act sets three tiers of fines, and which tier applies decides whether an infringement is expensive or existential.

**Tier 1: prohibited AI practices (Article 5).** Up to **EUR 35,000,000 or 7 percent of total worldwide annual turnover**, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). Social scoring, emotion recognition in the workplace, real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces.

**Tier 2: most operator obligations.** Up to **EUR 15,000,000 or 3 percent of annual turnover**, whichever is higher (Article 99(4)). That covers provider obligations under Article 16, authorised representatives (Article 22), importers (Article 23), distributors (Article 24), **deployer obligations under Article 26**, and **transparency obligations under Article 50**.

**Tier 3: incorrect information supplied to authorities.** Up to **EUR 7,500,000 or 1 percent of annual turnover**, whichever is higher (Article 99(5)). Supply the BNetzA with incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information and you land here.
sections.keyTakeaway: Three tiers: prohibited practices (EUR 35 million / 7 percent), standard obligations (EUR 15 million / 3 percent), incorrect information (EUR 7.5 million / 1 percent). Article 99(3) to (5).

sections.title: The SME rule: the lower amount applies
sections.content:
A large company pays the **higher** of the two amounts, the absolute figure or the percentage. For SMEs including start-ups, Article 99(6) turns that around: the **lower** amount applies.

The rule gets overlooked, and for a mid-sized business it decides everything. An undertaking with EUR 20 million in annual turnover faces at most EUR 1.4 million for a prohibited practice, equal to 7 percent. Not EUR 35 million.

The authority cannot pick a figure at will. Article 99(7) requires it to weigh **10 factors**, among them severity, the number of people affected, intent or negligence, company size, cooperation, and, expressly, **technical and organisational measures** under Article 99(7), point (g).

Documented AI governance counts in that assessment, meaning records of Article 4 training measures, a risk register, and an incident process. It does not guarantee a particular reduction.
sections.keyTakeaway: SME rule under Article 99(6): the lower amount applies. The 10 assessment factors in Article 99(7) include documented technical and organisational measures.

sections.title: Worked examples for SMEs
sections.content:
**Example A: machinery manufacturer with EUR 20 million in turnover**

- Tier 1, say emotion recognition at the factory gate: 7 percent = EUR 1.4 million. SME ceiling: EUR 1.4 million.
- Tier 2, say a missing risk assessment for HR AI: 3 percent = EUR 600,000. SME ceiling: EUR 600,000.
- Tier 3, incorrect information supplied to the BNetzA: 1 percent = EUR 200,000. SME ceiling: EUR 200,000.

**Example B: craft business with EUR 1.5 million in turnover**

- Tier 1: 7 percent = EUR 105,000. For a three-person business, that is existential.

In Germany the competent market-surveillance authority imposes sanctions under the German Act on Regulatory Offences (OWiG). An action before the administrative court is open under Article 99(10). Member States report to the Commission annually under Article 99(11).

The headline figure of EUR 35 million is generally not the applicable ceiling for a small or medium-sized organisation. In these examples the range runs from EUR 100,000 to EUR 1.4 million per category of infringement. Documented governance is one factor in the authority's assessment, not a guaranteed reduction.

For scale: the maximum fine for most obligations is 3% of total worldwide annual turnover under Article 99(4). For a medium-sized company with EUR 50 million in turnover, that is up to EUR 1.5 million. What ends up on the notice depends on proportionality and the documented measures.
sections.keyTakeaway: Illustrative range for an undertaking with EUR 20 million in turnover: EUR 200,000 to EUR 1.4 million. Documented governance is a relevant factor under Article 99(7), point (g), and does not predetermine the fine.

quiz.questionText: What is the maximum fine for using a prohibited AI practice under Article 5 of the AI Act?

answerOptions.text: Up to EUR 7.5 million or 1 percent of annual turnover
Up to EUR 15 million or 3 percent of annual turnover
Up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent of annual turnover, whichever is higher
Up to EUR 50 million or 10 percent of annual turnover

quiz.explanation: Article 99(3) of the AI Act provides for up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent of total worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices under Article 5, whichever is higher. For SMEs, Article 99(6) makes the lower amount applicable.

quiz.questionText: Which rule does Article 99(6) of the AI Act expressly apply to SMEs, including start-ups?

answerOptions.text: A fixed 50-percent reduction in the fine
The lower of the absolute amount and the percentage amount applies
Complete exemption from fines for the first three years
Fines are capped at EUR 10,000 regardless of the infringement

quiz.explanation: Article 99(6) turns the general rule around for SMEs: the lower of the absolute amount and the percentage amount applies. For an undertaking with EUR 20 million in turnover, the Tier 1 ceiling is EUR 1.4 million instead of EUR 35 million.

quiz.questionText: Which fine tier covers incorrect or misleading information that a company provides to a market-surveillance authority?

answerOptions.text: Tier 1: up to EUR 35 million or 7 percent
Tier 2: up to EUR 15 million or 3 percent
Tier 3: up to EUR 7.5 million or 1 percent
No fine tier applies; only a warning may be issued

quiz.explanation: Article 99(5) of the AI Act covers incorrect, incomplete, or misleading information supplied to notified bodies or competent national authorities, with fines of up to EUR 7.5 million or 1 percent of annual turnover. A company must cooperate with a BNetzA request. Protections for confidential information continue to apply.

lessons.title: AI regulatory sandboxes: free testing arrangements for SMEs
lessons.subtitle: What Article 57 provides, and why the original text, the AI Omnibus, and an operational service are three different things

sections.title: What an AI regulatory sandbox is under Article 57
sections.content:
You are building a high-risk AI system and want to talk to the authority before you place it on the market. That is what the **AI regulatory sandbox** is for: under Article 3, point (55), a controlled framework in which a competent authority lets a provider or prospective provider develop, train, validate, and, where appropriate, test an innovative AI system in real-world conditions.

The deadline for it has moved. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, applicable since 27 July 2026, sets **2 August 2027** in Article 57(1) as the date for at least one national AI regulatory sandbox.

Article 57 provides, among other things, for guidance, supervision, and a written exit report. Whether, when, and on what terms a German sandbox accepts applications is not in the deadline. It is in the enacted KI-MIG and in current information from the competent authority.
sections.keyTakeaway: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, applicable since 27 July 2026, moves the sandbox deadline to 2 August 2027. An operational German service is not proved by a deadline.

sections.title: What SMEs receive under the Regulation
sections.content:
Article 58(2), point (d), gives **SMEs including start-ups priority access**. And it costs nothing: an authority may recover only exceptional costs, and only in a fair and proportionate manner.

Three further commitments:

- **Protection from administrative fines:** where participants follow the sandbox plan in good faith, Article 57(12) bars authorities from imposing administrative fines for infringements of the Regulation. Liability under other Union and national law for damage caused to third parties remains unaffected.
- **Three-month decision period:** under Article 58(2), point (a), the authority must decide on an application within three months.
- **Support for later conformity assessment:** the written exit report is taken into account positively in a later conformity assessment under Article 57(7).

An organisation building a high-risk AI system, for recruitment or as an AI safety component in machinery, can talk to the authority **before** placing it on the market instead of arguing **afterwards**. This is an implementation option, not a substitute for the applicable legal duties.
sections.keyTakeaway: Priority for SMEs, free access, no administrative fines where the sandbox plan is followed in good faith, a decision within three months. A prospective provider of high-risk AI can weigh an application.

sections.title: Status in Germany: BNetzA, BfDI, and Hesse
sections.content:
A pilot is not a service. The German pilot project in 2025/2026 was run jointly by the **Federal Network Agency**, the **BfDI**, and the **Hessian Ministry for Digitalisation**, with two simulated start-up cases on the AI Act and the Medical Device Regulation (MDR). An open application process is not established by that.

The KI-MIG, in force since 29 July 2026, gives the BNetzA tasks in innovation support. The EU deadline of 2 August 2027 has been binding law since 27 July 2026.

Whether the BNetzA is already accepting applications is on the current authority website. Look there first, then write the application.
sections.keyTakeaway: The pilot project shows preparation, not an operational public service. Whether a German sandbox exists, and how to get into it, is a question for current official information.

quiz.questionText: What deadline did Parliament and the Council adopt through the AI Omnibus for at least one national AI regulatory sandbox?

answerOptions.text: By 2 February 2025
By 2 August 2025
By 2 August 2026 under the unchanged original text
By 2 August 2027 under the adopted AI Omnibus

quiz.explanation: The original text of Article 57(1) named 2 August 2026. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, applicable since 27 July 2026, moves the binding deadline to 2 August 2027.

quiz.questionText: Who receives priority access to an AI regulatory sandbox under Article 58(2), point (d), and what does access cost?

answerOptions.text: Large companies receive priority; access starts at EUR 50,000
SMEs, including start-ups, receive priority; access is free of charge
Only public authorities receive priority; access is free of charge
All companies have equal access; fees are scaled by turnover

quiz.explanation: Article 58(2), point (d), expressly gives SMEs including start-ups priority and makes access free of charge. Only exceptional costs may be recovered, in a fair and proportionate manner.

quiz.questionText: Which three authorities jointly ran Germany's AI regulatory-sandbox pilot project in 2025/2026?

answerOptions.text: BSI, BKA, and the Federal Chancellery
BaFin, BfArM, and the Federal Cartel Office
The Federal Network Agency, BfDI, and the Hessian Ministry for Digitalisation
DAkkS, TÜV, and the Fraunhofer Society

quiz.explanation: The Federal Network Agency, the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI), and the Hessian Ministry for Digitalisation ran the German pilot together, focused on start-up cases under the AI Act and the MDR.

lessons.title: Complaints, incident reports, and requests from the competent authority
lessons.subtitle: Incident reporting under Article 73, the right to lodge a complaint under Article 85, and the response plan for a mid-sized company
keyConcepts: right to lodge a complaint under Article 85
right to an explanation under Article 86

sections.title: What providers must report: Articles 72 and 73
sections.content:
Two days. A reporting period under Article 73 can be that short. Post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting reach providers once the high-risk rules apply. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 sets 2 December 2027 as the application date for standalone Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for high-risk systems embedded in products covered by Annex I.

**Article 72:** The post-market monitoring system collects performance data actively and systematically across the system's whole lifetime. The plan for it belongs in the technical documentation.

**Article 73:** Once the provision applies, a serious incident goes to the competent market-surveillance authority. The Regulation generally specifies 15 days, 10 days for certain incidents resulting in death, and two days for a widespread infringement or disruption of critical infrastructure. Product-safety and data-protection law may independently trigger their own reporting channels and periods, and those already apply.

Which German authority and which channel are operational in a particular case, these periods do not say.
sections.keyTakeaway: Articles 72 and 73 belong to the high-risk regime. Confirm the application date, the competent authority, and any parallel reporting duties before an incident, not after it.

sections.title: Who may report you: the right to lodge a complaint under Article 85
sections.content:
Anyone may report you. **Article 85 of the AI Act:** any natural or legal person that has grounds to consider that there has been an infringement may lodge a complaint with the relevant market-surveillance authority.

Since 29 July 2026 the KI-MIG has made the **BNetzA the single point of contact and complaints body** where no sectoral authority has jurisdiction. Before lodging a complaint, check the applicable sectoral law and current information from the authorities anyway, to confirm jurisdiction and the active channel.

**Related: Article 86.** Subject to its conditions, it gives a right to a clear and meaningful explanation of the role that a high-risk system listed in Annex III played in the decision-making procedure. It is not a general right to an explanation for every AI output.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 85 opens a complaint to the relevant market-surveillance authority to any person. Confirm the responsible German authority and its active channel under the enacted KI-MIG, applicable sectoral law, and current official information.

sections.title: Authority request: a five-step response plan
sections.content:
The authority may do a great deal. Under Article 74 it obtains full access to documentation and to training, validation, and testing data sets, including through APIs (Article 74(12)). **Source code** it gets only on a reasoned request, and only after other testing or audit procedures have been exhausted or proved insufficient (Article 74(13)).

If it finds non-compliance, it requires the relevant operator to take corrective action. The period is **no more than 15 working days** under Article 79(2). For non-compliance with the prohibition in Article 5, the Union safeguard procedure shortens the objection period to 30 days under Article 81.

**Your initial response plan (an implementation control, not a statutory five-step format):**

1. **Acknowledge in writing** and record the deadline. Never hand over source code or training data on reflex. Involve legal counsel.
2. **Open an incident log.** Date, request, people involved, information communicated.
3. **Confirm jurisdiction.** Is the BNetzA really competent, or a sectoral authority such as BaFin, BfArM, or an LMA?
4. **Assemble compliance records:** records of Article 4 training measures, the risk assessment, post-market monitoring records, and the declaration of conformity. They may evidence technical and organisational measures under Article 99(7), point (g); they do not guarantee a lower fine.
5. **Cooperate without giving incorrect information.** Incorrect or incomplete information falls within Tier 3, up to EUR 7.5 million or 1 percent under Article 99(5).

Preparation beats panic. Prepared records, an identified lawyer, and a designated spokesperson carry the first 48 hours. They do not remove the legal duties or determine the authority's response.
sections.keyTakeaway: The corrective-action period is no more than 15 working days under Article 79(2). The five-step implementation plan: acknowledge, log, confirm jurisdiction, assemble records, and cooperate without giving incorrect information.

quiz.questionText: Within what period must a provider of a high-risk AI system report a serious incident resulting in death?

answerOptions.text: Two days after becoming aware
10 days after establishing the suspected causal link
15 days after becoming aware
72 hours after becoming aware

quiz.explanation: Article 73(4) of the AI Act sets a shortened 10-day reporting period where a person dies, counted from the date on which the causal link between the high-risk AI system and the incident has been established or its reasonable likelihood identified. The general period is 15 days under paragraph 2, and two days for a widespread infringement under paragraph 3.

quiz.questionText: Who may lodge a complaint with a market-surveillance authority under Article 85 of the AI Act?

answerOptions.text: Only directly affected natural persons represented by a lawyer
Only recognised consumer organisations and trade unions
Any natural or legal person that has grounds to consider that there has been an infringement
Only Member States acting through the single point of contact

quiz.explanation: Article 85 of the AI Act lets any natural or legal person lodge a complaint where they have grounds to consider that an infringement has occurred. No special standing, no lawyer required. Whistleblowers are additionally protected under Article 87 and Directive (EU) 2019/1937.

quiz.questionText: When may a market-surveillance authority request access to the source code of a high-risk AI system under Article 74(13)?

answerOptions.text: At any time and without stating reasons
Only after a criminal complaint has been filed against the provider
Only on a reasoned request and when other testing or audit procedures have been exhausted or proved insufficient
Only under a court order

quiz.explanation: Article 74(13) sets two cumulative conditions for access to source code: the access must be necessary to assess conformity, and the testing or audit procedures based on data and documentation supplied by the provider must have been exhausted or proved insufficient.
